card.thesis: At banks, stretching a new-car loan by an extra year has barely raised the interest rate, so nearly all the added cost comes from paying interest longer.
card.overturns: "Longer car loans cost more mainly because lenders charge a much higher rate."

claim: In every quarter since the Federal Reserve began publishing a 72-month new-car loan rate at commercial banks (44 quarters, August 2015 to May 2026), the 72-month rate averaged only 0.097 points above the 60-month rate, never more than 0.52 points, and was equal to or lower than the 60-month rate in 34.1% of quarters; in May 2026 it was 6.97% versus 7.14%. On a $30,000 loan at the 7.14% 60-month rate, adding the extra year alone adds about $1,210 of interest, while charging the average term premium adds only about $101 more, so about 7.7% of the extra interest comes from a higher rate and the rest from paying longer. The cost of a longer car loan is time, not the rate. This is history, not a forecast.

Use only dates where both have a value: 44 quarters, 2015-08-01 through 2026-05-01. Count of those dates.

interest(r, n) on $30,000 = n * 30000*i/(1-(1+i)^-n) - 30000 with i = r/1200 (standard level-payment amortization). term_effect = interest(7.14, 72) - interest(7.14, 60), rounded to the dollar (7.14 = latest 60-month rate).

interest(r, n) on $30,000 = n * 30000*i/(1-(1+i)^-n) - 30000 with i = r/1200 (standard level-payment amortization). rate_effect = interest(7.14 + m, 72) - interest(7.14, 72), where m is the unrounded mean_premium_72_vs_60; rounded to the dollar.
100 * rate_effect / (term_effect + rate_effect), using unrounded values, rounded to 0.1.

series.provider: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

assumptions: Loan of $30,000, level monthly payments, no fees, no early payoff; rates are the bank survey averages, not any one borrower's offer.
The average term premium over 2015-2026 is applied to the latest 60-month rate to split extra interest into a term part and a rate part.
The two rates come from the same survey of commercial banks; dealer-arranged and captive-finance loans are not covered.
limits: History, not a forecast. The series covers commercial banks only; borrowers who take longer loans may have different credit profiles, and captive lenders, credit unions and dealer markups can price terms differently. Longer loans also raise the risk of owing more than the car is worth, which this measure does not capture.
